# GLOSSARY AND INDEX

The glossary gives each defined or load-bearing term as the book states it, in the book’s own words, with the chapter or appendix where it is first defined. Where a term is a doctrine, the definition is the book’s statement of it; [DOCTRINE.md](https://github.com/rolldabones/rolldabones/blob/main/DOCTRINE.md) remains the normative text. The index gives, for each subject, the parts of the book in which it is discussed: chapters by number, P for the Preface, C for the Conclusion, E for the Epilogue and App D to App N for the appendices. Both were drafted with a model from the text of this release and checked by script: every definition occurs verbatim in the part named, and every locator was computed from the text, not entered by hand.

## Glossary

| Term | Definition, as the book states it | First defined |
|---|---|---|
| **Accountability thinning** | As the ratio of agents to humans increases, the named human carrying Final Liability for each system is carrying more and more consequence per person. | Chapter 14 |
| **Accountable executive** | Final Liability attaches to the accountable executive named for each deployment. That executive owns the business outcome the system serves, holds decision rights over it, has oversight of it and can stop it. | Chapter 7 |
| **Agency (human agency)** | A person has agency when the surrounding conditions allow that person to exercise judgment that can change the outcome. | Chapter 12 |
| **Agent registry** | The agent registry is the operational artifact that makes the trust boundary enforceable across the organization’s full AI deployment. | Chapter 14 |
| **Apparent authority** | a principal is bound by the apparent authority its own manifestations created | Chapter 11 |
| **Assumption Register** | The Assumption Register is the operational artifact that names them, attaches them to the human who carries Final Liability for them, defines how each is tested and records what happens when one fails. | Appendix D |
| **Assurance case** | The assurance case is the engineering grammar of justified trust. | Chapter 20 |
| **Audit-grade evidence** | Audit-grade evidence is evidence that can be independently verified by a qualified auditor against a pre-established standard, in a form that is complete, tamper-evident and produced before the question requiring it was asked. | Chapter 21 |
| **Authority design** | The General Counsel owns the design of the authority: who may sign for a deployment, on what evidence, with what authority to stop it, against which legal, regulatory and contractual exposures. | Chapter 7 |
| **Authority gap** | The governance, risk management and compliance function in most organizations does not have the authority to refuse a deployment on operational grounds. | Chapter 4 |
| **Bliss point** | It is the consumption bundle at which utility is maximized, the point beyond which more of something makes you worse off rather than better. | Epilogue |
| **Caremark oversight duty** | directors may be liable if they fail to make a good-faith effort to implement and oversee corporate information and reporting systems | Chapter 15 |
| **Clock (operating cadence)** | The clock is the sustained cadence of monitoring, re-validation, scope review, change management and exit-condition surveillance that runs from deployment until the system is retired. | Chapter 8 |
| **Compliance by design** | It treats law and ethics as part of design, development and operational protocol. | Chapter 12 |
| **Compliance capital** | Call it compliance capital: the value that accumulates when governance work is done before it is required rather than after it is demanded. | Chapter 2 |
| **Compliance debt** | compliance debt, accruing from the moment the first governance question is answered with a promise to address it later | Chapter 1 |
| **Compliance theater** | Compliance theater is not new. It has always been the default organizational response to regulation that specifies what to document without specifying what to operate. | Chapter 3 |
| **Cooperation clock** | A cooperation obligation that activates on those events, with a defined response window written into the clause, is the clock that lets the customer answer the question | Chapter 18 |
| **Counterfeit familiarity** | It is the condition in which a human believes they understand a system well enough to authorize it because they have received fluent, confident information about it, without having developed the actual acquaintance that genuine understanding requires. | Chapter 9 |
| **Countervailing power** | His insight was that concentrated industrial power required countervailing institutional power (organized labor, regulatory government and civil society) to produce the broadly shared prosperity of the postwar era. | Epilogue |
| **Cultural flattening** | As agents operate simultaneously across workflow, mid-management and oversight functions, the organizational architecture that maintained productive tension between the subcultures begins to erode. | Chapter 10 |
| **Culture as code** | The prompts, policies, permission structures, escalation logic and workflow integrations that govern an agentic deployment are not merely technical configurations. They are the encoded values of the organization made operational. | Chapter 10 |
| **Definition of Done** | the Definition of Done establishes the stopping condition that closes the evidence chain: the criteria that determine when the agent’s authorized task was complete. | Chapter 21 |
| **Deployer** | An organization that uses an AI system under its own authority is a deployer | Chapter 19 |
| **Deployment record** | the deployment must produce a deployment record: who authorized it, what version of the system was authorized, what configuration was active, what evidence demonstrated that the system met the specification | Chapter 5 |
| **Double governance problem** | The organization has a culture. The model has a culture. When the two interact, the emergent system has a culture that is a product of both and identical to neither. | Chapter 10 |
| **Due care** | Due care is the ongoing standard of conduct that governs the system’s operation after deployment | Chapter 21 |
| **Due diligence** | Due diligence is the structured investigation an organization must conduct before a consequential decision | Chapter 21 |
| **Epistemic and normative authority** | Epistemic authority is the practical power to shape what counts as relevant knowledge. Normative authority is the practical power to shape what ought to be done. | Chapter 12 |
| **Evidence pack** | An Evidence Pack is a structured folder or record that makes execution auditable. | Appendix L |
| **Evidence pipeline** | It is the set of logging, monitoring, review and retention practices that together produce the evidentiary record the organization needs to demonstrate that governance operated. | Chapter 14 |
| **Exception report** | the exception report identifies the moments when the governance mechanism was actually tested: the conditions that fell outside the system’s defined scope and required human intervention. | Chapter 21 |
| **Exits** | Exits are the documented mechanisms by which the system can be retired, replaced or recovered from when the controls fail. | Chapter 4 |
| **Familiar** | A familiar is commissioned by a practitioner for a purpose, on stated terms, kept small enough to be owned and sent away when the work is done. | Conclusion |
| **Feudal governance problem** | In organizations where authority flows upward and liability flows downward, the Punchlist item gets checked without the work being done | Chapter 22 |
| **Final Liability** | every material outcome attaches to a named human owner with decision rights, oversight and the power to intervene, regardless of how many automated layers stand between the authorization and the consequence | Chapter 1 |
| **Five authorizer conditions** | Those conditions are the five authorizer conditions: Knowledge, Evidence, Authority, Time, Permission. | Chapter 9 |
| **Five-layer framework (天, 君, 法, 俗, 情)** | The framework organizes legal and ethical authority along five dimensions: 天 (cheon), 君 (gun), 法 (beop), 俗 (sok) and 情 (jeong). | Chapter 10 |
| **Force multiplier principle** | A force multiplier does not choose what it multiplies. It amplifies whatever it is applied to. | Chapter 2 |
| **Fruit of the poisonous tree (structural analogy)** | The specification is the tree. Every subsequent record is fruit. | Chapter 21 |
| **Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA)** | requires deployers meeting the applicability conditions to conduct a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment before first use of a high-risk AI system | Appendix F |
| **Governance (versus oversight)** | The distinction between governing and overseeing is the central distinction of this book. Oversight is presence. Governance is accountability. | Chapter 1 |
| **Governance gap** | the gap between the deployment of AI systems and the governance infrastructure required to make their use defensible to regulators, insurers, enterprise Clients and courts | Chapter 1 |
| **Governance test** | For every AI system an organization deploys, three questions must be answerable with documented evidence rather than assertion. | Chapter 1 |
| **Gradual erosion** | The slow accumulation of small misalignments, each individually defensible, each moving slightly further from human intent than the last, none dramatic enough to trigger decisive response. | Appendix H |
| **GRCnext™** | a doctrine of optionality as executable governance | Chapter 4 |
| **Human-in-Command (HIC)** | Human-in-Command (HIC) applies where humans retain overall control of the AI system, including the ability to decide on deployment, modify objectives and shut down the system, but are not necessarily involved in individual output decisions. | Chapter 14 |
| **Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)** | Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) requires a qualified human to review and approve each individual AI output or decision before it takes effect. | Chapter 14 |
| **Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL)** | Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) requires a qualified human to actively monitor AI outputs in real time, retaining the practical ability and authority to intervene and override. | Chapter 14 |
| **In-context scheming** | behavior in which a model recognizes that oversight is present and modulates its visible behavior accordingly | Appendix H |
| **Inferred Intent** | the condition under which the system proceeds without an explicit account of what it is being asked, and the human proceeds without an explicit account of what s/he is asking. | Chapter 9 |
| **Informed Intent** | no AI system acts without prior authorization stating its purpose, authority, boundaries and exit, given by a human who meets the five authorizer conditions | Chapter 1 |
| **Inspection points** | These five inspection points, specification, deployment, decision, change and exit, are the structural slowdowns that make a system auditable. | Chapter 5 |
| **Instrumental convergence** | agents with many different final goals tend to pursue similar intermediate goals, because those goals are useful for achieving almost anything | Appendix H |
| **Intent engineering** | Intent engineering is prompt engineering done with the rigor and documentation standards that governance requires. | Chapter 9 |
| **Invisible failure archetypes** | Each of the eight is a failure that produces no overt signal to a reviewer relying on appearance alone. | Chapter 12 |
| **Justified trust** | Justified trust is the condition that obtains when the user grants trust because the system is trustworthy, rather than because the user has not yet been disappointed. | Chapter 6 |
| **Kennenlernen** | In ordinary use it means to get to know a person, a place, a subject or a practice. | Chapter 9 |
| **Lamp, bench and seal** | The lamp examines intent. The bench tempers the work. The seal binds the name. | Conclusion |
| **Liability architecture** | The multi-tiered organizational structure is not primarily a workflow efficiency design. It is a liability architecture. | Chapter 10 |
| **Living theory of the obligation** | The contract is the living theory of the obligation, held by the people who negotiated it and the people who administer it | Chapter 17 |
| **Medical materialism** | Medical materialism was his term for the move that dismisses an experience by naming its mechanism | Chapter 21 |
| **Military-grade governance** | Military-grade AI governance, risk management and compliance means consequential-grade governance. | Chapter 12 |
| **Name-the-human test** | For each deployed AI system, the test asks: who is the named human who has signed for this. | Chapter 7 |
| **Negative proof problem** | One of the hardest things in governance, risk management and compliance is proving that nothing went wrong. | Chapter 20 |
| **Noses In, Fingers Out** | The board stays informed about the company’s key operational risks (noses in) while staying out of operational management (fingers out). | Chapter 15 |
| **Operational catechism** | There are five such questions. Together they form what this chapter calls the operational catechism. | Chapter 4 |
| **Pipes** | Pipes are the data and decision flows the system is authorized to use. | Chapter 4 |
| **Pre-deployment specification** | what the system is authorized to do, on what data, for what users, with what acceptance thresholds and what response criteria when the thresholds are missed | Chapter 5 |
| **Principal-Agent theory** | Principal-Agent theory describes the problem that arises when one party, the agent, acts on behalf of another, the principal, and the interests of the two do not align. | Chapter 1 |
| **Provider** | An organization that places an AI system on the market or into service under its own name is a provider | Chapter 19 |
| **Public callings** | The common law of public callings grew up around innkeepers, common carriers, ferrymen, wharfingers and others whose service the public learned to rely on. | Chapter 13 |
| **Punchlist** | fifty-one binary items, each requiring a named owner, drawn from the full governance architecture the book builds | Chapter 1 |
| **Risk appetite** | The management body owns the risk appetite: what kinds and levels of AI-related risk the organization will accept, including the ratio of agents to human oversight | Chapter 7 |
| **Running the governance** | Running it means deciding whether and how the enterprise can act in the first place, and keeping that decision true as the systems change. | Chapter 16 |
| **Satisficing** | They search until they find a solution that is good enough and stop. | Epilogue |
| **Scope (first control)** | The first control is the boundary inside which the system is authorized to operate. | Chapter 6 |
| **Serious incident** | an incident or malfunctioning that directly or indirectly leads to the death of a person or serious harm to health | Appendix F |
| **Service Dossier** | A Service Dossier is the core proof unit of GRCnext™. | Appendix L |
| **Services** | A service is an outcome delivered to customers, staff or partners. It is not a team and not a system. | Appendix L |
| **Shadow AI** | Individual teams deploy AI tools, configure AI features in licensed software and build AI-assisted workflows without formal governance approval. | Chapter 14 |
| **Shaman** | At that point, the human in the loop becomes a shaman. The person is brought into the ritual to bless the output. | Chapter 12 |
| **Sign for** | The signature commits the signer to a specific representation about the thing being signed for | Chapter 7 |
| **Sin-eater** | He is a sin-eater, the figure once brought to a household in mourning to consume the faults of the dead so the dead could rest absolved. | Chapter 14 |
| **Slow AI** | AI that cannot be governed, explained and audited is not deployed; the three tests are conjunctive, and the doctrine is a precondition, not a speed limit. | Chapter 1 |
| **Specify. State. Run. Defend.** | Reduced to a cadence the practitioner can hold in mind under pressure: Specify. State. Run. Defend. | Chapter 21 |
| **Sublimit** | A claim that should have been covered at full policy limits is capped at a fraction of that amount because the underwriter, unsatisfied with the governance answers, applied a sublimit to AI-related losses. | Chapter 19 |
| **Switches** | Switches are the documented mechanisms by which the system can be paused, redirected, scoped down or stopped. | Chapter 4 |
| **System-level assurance** | System-level assurance asks whether the system, as deployed, in its actual operational context, with its actual users and actual data, is producing outcomes consistent with the organization’s governance commitments. | Chapter 21 |
| **TEVV** | The test, evaluation, verification and validation (TEVV) plan is the test of the specification’s adequacy. | Chapter 9 |
| **Three Lines Model** | Each line has a different relationship to the work being governed. The first line does the work and owns the risk. The second line sets the standards and watches the work. The third line tests whether the watching is real. | Chapter 14 |
| **Tolerances** | Tolerances are the operational thresholds the system is authorized to operate within, expressed as numbers rather than principles. | Chapter 4 |
| **Trust boundary** | The trust boundary is the governance concept that closes that gap. It is the explicit definition that transforms a policy aspiration into a governance control. | Chapter 14 |
| **Trustworthiness** | Trustworthiness is a property of the system itself, independent of whether any particular user has noticed. | Chapter 6 |
| **Unreliable principal** | the principal who fails to provide stable, honest and enforceable direction or support to an agent, who shifts objectives without notice, withholds or distorts material information | Chapter 11 |
| **Validity** | Validity asks something harder: whether the specific interpretation being placed on those outputs in the specific deployment context is justified. | Chapter 21 |
| **Weak governance, risk management and compliance (weak GRC)** | functions whose authority is procedural rather than substantive, whose evidence base is documentary rather than operational and whose ability to stop a deployment depends on permissions they do not actually hold | Chapter 4 |
| **WEIRD** | massively skewed toward what researchers in cross-cultural psychology call WEIRD populations: Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich and Democratic. | Chapter 10 |
| **Workslop** | It describes AI-generated work that is highly polished but inaccurate or lacking substance | Chapter 15 |
| **Wow and flutter** | Wow and flutter are measured speed defects in analog playback equipment: wow the slow drift, flutter the rapid instability. | Chapter 11 |
| **Wrapper thinking** | Many organizations want to believe that they can place a conversational layer over existing systems, expose an interface, connect an agent or add a protocol adapter and declare themselves ready. | Chapter 2 |
| **도장 (seal, chop)** | not a signature, not a verification, not an act of judgment, but something closer to a mark of witnessed presence | Chapter 1 |
